questions.q: Why does this lesson say a vague statement like "the system must be fast" keeps recurring even on teams that know better?
options: Because Salesforce Setup does not allow numeric performance targets to be entered anywhere
Because it's genuinely harder to state a specific number and condition than to gesture at a quality, and a vague statement is easier to avoid disagreeing with in a meeting
Because metrics and targets are only required for compliance NFRs, not performance NFRs
Because this mistake only happens on teams with no architect involved
questions.explain: Precision requires committing to a specific, checkable number and condition, which is harder and more exposing than a vague statement that's easy for everyone in the room to nod along with.

questions.q: Why is a successful demo or pilot described as insufficient proof that an NFR is satisfied?
options: Because demos are always run with fabricated data
Because pilots are illegal under most compliance regulations
Because Salesforce disables governor limits during any demo
Because a demo or pilot typically runs under easy, low-volume, no-failure conditions, which tells you nothing about behavior at real volume, under real attack, or when something actually fails
questions.explain: The conditions that would actually stress-test an NFR — a volume spike, an outage, an audit — are rare and easy to overlook, so passing under easy demo conditions says nothing about whether the NFR holds under the conditions that actually matter.

questions.q: What is the "vendor/implementation gap" mistake this lesson names?
options: Assuming Salesforce's own platform-level certifications and published information automatically make a specific customer's implementation compliant or available to the same standard, when the customer's own design choices are a separate responsibility
A technical bug where Salesforce's API version doesn't match the client application's version
A pricing discrepancy between list price and the final signed contract
A governor-limit mismatch between sandbox and production environments
questions.explain: This mistake, named directly in Lessons 7 and 12, is believing the platform vendor's own certifications or published status information automatically cover a specific customer's own implementation choices — they don't, and the distinction is often blurred.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does "deciding a design without ever stating which NFR drove it" keep happening even when the architect genuinely had good reasons?
options: Because Salesforce Flow does not support documentation comments
Because design decisions are never actually connected to any NFR in real projects

Because the architect making the decision usually understands the reasoning in the moment, and the gap only becomes visible once someone else has to maintain or defend the decision later without that context
Because this mistake can only occur in multi-tenant Salesforce orgs
questions.explain: The reasoning is real and clear to the person who made the decision at the time — the problem surfaces only later, for a different person trying to understand or defend the decision without that same context, which is exactly why Lesson 9's trace pattern requires writing it down.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say "we'll just do both, fully" is usually a sign a real NFR conflict was never actually engaged with?
options: Because doing both fully is always technically impossible on the Salesforce platform

Because naming a real trade-off requires someone to accept a specific cost or risk, which is uncomfortable to put a name on, compared to an unbounded promise that sounds better but isn't actually true
Because Salesforce forbids resolving NFR conflicts without written legal approval
Because this phrase only ever appears in compliance NFR discussions
questions.explain: A real trade-off means accepting a specific, named cost — which is uncomfortable to commit to compared to an unbounded, feel-good promise that both NFRs will be fully satisfied, even when that promise isn't actually realistic.
